detail.longDescription:
Hey everyone, Daniel here. For those unfamiliar, Reitti is an open-source,
privacy-focused, self-hosted location tracker and Google Timeline alternative.
It ingests data from open clients like OwnTracks or GPSLogger, geotags your
Immich photos, and keeps your travel history completely under your own control.
Over the past few weeks, several updates have landed. The main addition is
something I would have done way earlier, but never found the time for: a
completely reworked Statistics page. These updates also include a new fitness
integration, major visit detection improvements, and substantial security
hardening, thanks to a lot of PRs and security advisories I received over the
last month. Here is an overview of what is new. — ### The New Statistics Page
The statistics section used to be just a handful of simple charts. It has been
rebuilt into a movement and lifestyle report that you can view across months,
years, or your entire history: * Key Figures: Distance totals, percentage of
weekday time spent at home, places visited (including how many were new), nights
away from home, and your Eddington number for distance. * Weekday vs. Weekend
Habits: A side-by-side comparison showing how routines change between workdays
and weekends (daily distances, typical departure/return times, stop counts). *
Movement Radar: A radar chart showing visited locations organized by direction
and distance relative to home. * Day Classification Calendar: Days are
automatically categorized (Commute, Wander, Travel, Home, or Untracked), with
low-data days faded out so they do not distort your overall metrics. * Routines
and Transport Breakdown: Recurring locations, stay durations, and trip
breakdowns (time, distance, count, average speed) across transport modes.
[https://discuss.tchncs.de/pictrs/image/2dd67643-3087-4300-87d3-cea09926a309.png]
I was also able to reuse several components from the new statistics page to
improve the visuals and usefulness of the aggregated timeline view when looking
at more than two weeks of data at once. You can now click directly on a day row
inside the chart to inspect it, and your top places for that period are also
selectable.
[https://discuss.tchncs.de/pictrs/image/22ef9032-73a3-483d-a48d-65af0748940c.png]
— ### Intervals.icu / Garmin Integration If you track activities like running,
cycling, or hiking with a Garmin watch, you no longer have to export and upload
FIT files manually. Reitti now supports background syncing via Intervals.icu:
Garmin Watch -> Garmin Connect -> Intervals.icu -> Reitti Once configured with
an API key, Reitti runs an initial historical import and continues syncing new
activities automatically in the background. (Note: Due to Strava’s API terms,
activities originating strictly from Strava cannot be forwarded via this
bridge). — ### Smarter Visit & Transport Detection The data processing pipeline
received several core improvements: * Speed-Based Visit Detection: Instead of
relying on rigid time and distance guards when dealing with sparse points (like
battery-saver modes in OwnTracks), Reitti now derives stationary visits based on
speed between points. This makes detection significantly more accurate. * Better
Transition Handling: Detection logic handles intermediate edge cases much more
gracefully, preventing anomalous slowdowns during fast travel (like temporary
traffic slowdowns) from misclassifying trips. — ### A Note on Security and
Hardening Security has been a major focus recently. In one release alone, an
external contributor submitted 16 security-related PRs addressing various areas
across the codebase. Alongside those, several reported advisories were resolved,
including issues around share-link scoping, file uploads, and map style
handling. Most of these issues boil down to scenarios where client-side code
could be executed in the context of another user if triggered. Because of that,
the baseline assumption remains: you should trust the users on your instance. If
your instance is exposed to the internet, upgrading to the latest version is
always a good idea. I will continue doing my best to fix these types of
vulnerabilities as they are found, provided the fixes do not get in the way of
usability. — ### Other Notes Arch Linux / AUR: Huge thanks to hashworks for
packaging Reitti for Arch Linux! It is available directly in the AUR at
aur.archlinux.org/packages/reitti. This one really made my day after I found it.
— ### What’s Next: Notifications (Looking for Community Input!) For upcoming
releases, I want to introduce a notification mechanism. Some potential use
cases: * System events: Version upgrade alerts, background job updates (e.g.,
successful or failed imports). * Memory triggers: Automatic detection when you
stay overnight away from home, paired with a gentle nudge to turn that trip into
a Memory. * Workflow triggers: Alerts for geofence crossings of users (if I ever
implement geofences) or when a device did not report for x hours. Right now, I
am looking at built-in in-app notifications and third-party services like
ntfy.sh [https://ntfy.sh/]. What other notification channels do you rely on in
your self-hosted stack (Gotify, Webhooks, Apprise, Telegram, email)? And what
kind of events or lifestyle nudges would actually be useful to you without
feeling like spam? — ### Links & Community * Source Code:
github.com/dedicatedcode/reitti [https://github.com/dedicatedcode/reitti] *
Release Notes: GitHub Releases
[https://github.com/dedicatedcode/reitti/releases] * Documentation:
dedicatedcode.com/projects/reitti/latest/
[https://www.dedicatedcode.com/projects/reitti/latest/] * IRC: Drop by #reitti
on Libera Chat [https://libera.chat/] if you want to chat, ask questions, or
hang out. * Support the Project: If you find Reitti useful and want to help
support development, you can find me on Patreon [https://patreon.com/reitti] and
Ko-fi [https://ko-fi.com/reitti]. Feedback, questions, and ideas are always
welcome! — Daniel — ### AI Project Disclosure * Implementation (Assisted): I use
AI to write repetitive boilerplate code that is tedious to write manually. The
majority of the codebase is written directly by me, and all generated code is
reviewed and tested by me. * Testing (Pair): Approximately an even split between
human-authored tests and AI-assisted generation for test scenarios and edge
cases. * Documentation (Assisted): I use AI as an editing tool to help refine
phrasing, documentation, and release notes into clean English. All content,
technical decisions, and structure are mine.
